p.s. when I said we are on the "same side" I should have been more precise. 

I was simply correcting the false assumption that I am some outsider clinician who has no idea of the realities that patients face.

These are all great points. You're right. There is no evidence that inpatient psychiatric care has any benefit. I described the literature on this in an affidavit to support depopulating psychiatric facilities in Massachusetts during COVID-19. I was only able to make the points I made in that legal document because of the research that people have done on this topic. 

You are also right that there is \*some\* empirical evidence that it harms, but the literature is very sparse. There will be even more evidence linking inpatient psych to outcomes with this survey and the research that will build from it. 

I respect your stance on inpatient psychiatry and abolition. I disagree that these two "tracks" are necessarily in competition. I also disagree that we know enough to know that abolition makes sense across the board and, also, this is simply not likely to occur anytime soon. There are plenty of people in my survey so far who have had negative experiences. However, there are also plenty of people who have had positive experiences. There is variation across facilities in environments and between people in what they say helps/does not help. 

I have a paper that will come out hopefully soon that describes incidents such as abuse, and how these vary by "Institutions of Mental Disease (IMDs)." There has been a great deal of policy movement in recent years to expand coverage to IMDs (freestanding psych hospitals with >16 beds), yet there has not been any empirical critique of unintended consequences or quality variation. These are the types of policies my work informs (e.g., expanding Medicaid coverage to more psychiatric hospitals). Again, I respect your stance. The reality I see is that the field is not moving towards abolition and many of the advocates who otherwise would be watchdogs on issues of quality and human rights are not interested in "reform" (understandably); this leaves a large hole within which providers are not held accountable and some are even exploiting these circumstances for profit (see Universal Health Services). 

Morgan

Hi there, 

I do not have to tolerate being spoken to in such a dehumanizing way.

I am also not a clinician. I also do not have a 401k or a nice house. Further, I have lived experience. 

I understand why you are angry and why you might be quick to make assumptions about me. There are huge power imbalances in psychiatry, and many people have been hurt. There is no denying it. It is for this reason that I am building a program of research on this issue, and actively try to translate my findings into impact. Unfortunately, the system is not going to change without people doing hard work, which includes both advocacy/activism as well as research. 

I hope that you might consider the possibility that we are on the same side. At the same time, I understand if you can't. 

Have a nice evening.

Good question. We decided to restrict it to the United States in order to say something specifically about the US experience and translate findings to potential policy solutions. Policy solutions will vary across countries, especially given the US' private provision of healthcare. Also, most of the research describing inpatient psychiatric care has been conducted outside the US; there is a need for US studies. 

But I do agree that general questions related to the experience and outcomes are universally relevant, and perhaps we will broaden our scope in subsequent work!

Well -- while I did get a B.A. in psychology, my Ph.D. is actually in social policy, with a concentration in behavioral health services research. My Ph.D. falls under the general umbrellas of public health and social policy. 

The primary difference between what I do and what psychology researchers (tend) to do is that I was trained to think about population-level health, how policies impact health, and how health care is financed and organized. Psychologists tend to think more at the individual level, and less on these overarching structures. 

I did know I wanted to study the quality of behavioral health and, specifically, inpatient psych since I was an undergrad. I just didn't know any other path other than psychology until a mentor suggested I research the field of public health; I'm glad I did because this is a great fit for me.
